scenes.narration: A subway map. The first time you reach a station is already the fastest way there. Always. Why?
Pattern six of ten in the NBX Studio Dojo: Breadth-First Search. It finds the shortest path, and the only reason it works is the order it visits things in.

scenes.headline: The words that [give it away]
scenes.caption: signals in the question
scenes.narration: Your giveaway word is ^shortest, and it's almost always literally in the question. ^Minimum steps, or fewest moves, which is the same thing wearing a different hat. ^Level order, when a tree has to be read row by row. ^Nearest, or closest, which means distance again. ^But if the edges have different weights, plain breadth-first search is wrong and you want Dijkstra instead. ^And if you only need to know whether a path exists at all, depth-first is cheaper. Shortest is the word. Everything else follows from it.
scenes.premise: Words lifted straight out of the question, and the pattern each one points at. Red means the signal rules this pattern OUT.

scenes.headline: Five stops, [one map]
scenes.caption: the network, laid out by distance
scenes.narration: You're standing at ^station A and you need to reach station E in as few stops as possible. That map connects ^A to B, ^A to C as well, ^B to D, ^C to D, and finally ^D to E. You could hop on any train and hope, and you might get there eventually by a scenic route. Breadth-first search is more disciplined, because it refuses to guess: it checks every station one stop away before it looks at any station two stops away.
scenes.premise: A subway map. Each circle is a station, each line a direct connection, and the badge on a station is how many stops it sits from A.

scenes.headline: A queue, and a [visited set]
scenes.caption: the two things you carry
scenes.narration: ^Standing at A, |the queue is our to-visit list, and it holds one entry: +visit A, zero stops out. A deque is a list that's fast at both ends. |Visited is the set of stations already queued, and %it starts holding A. %One queue, one set. Every breadth-first search has both: the queue decides the order, and the set stops you going round in circles.

lines.detail: The to-visit list, starting at A, zero stops away.
Everything we have already queued, so we never queue it twice.

scenes.premise: A subway map. Each circle is a station, each line a direct connection, and the badge on a station is how many stops it sits from A.

scenes.headline: Take from the [front]
scenes.caption: first in, first out
scenes.narration: |While the queue holds anything, keep going. |Queue dot popleft takes the station at the front and removes it. Front, not back, and that one word is the whole difference between this and the previous pattern. ^We take A, at %zero stops. |Is A our destination? Not yet. A stack hands back the most recent station; a queue hands back the earliest, which means the nearest, and that's why the answer comes out shortest.

lines.detail: Keep going while anything is still waiting.
Take from the FRONT. Earliest added, nearest.

scenes.premise: A subway map. Each circle is a station, each line a direct connection, and the badge on a station is how many stops it sits from A.

scenes.headline: Everything [one stop away]
scenes.caption: the first ring
scenes.narration: |Now the neighbours. A connects to B and to C. |For each one we ask whether we've seen it before, and neither of them has been. |So we mark them visited, |and push them onto the back of the queue, each carrying zero plus one, which is one stop. ^B goes on. ^C goes on. +The queue now holds B and C, +both at distance one. That's the first ring of the ripple, and nothing at distance two can be looked at until both of these have been.

lines.detail: Look at everything this station connects to.
Mark it, so nobody queues it again.
Push it on the BACK, one stop further out.

scenes.premise: A subway map. Each circle is a station, each line a direct connection, and the badge on a station is how many stops it sits from A.

scenes.narration: ^Straight from the Dojo. B and C are both in the to-visit list. Which do we check first? ^C, added last. ^B, added first. ^Or whichever looks closer to E. Have a think, and pause the video if you'd like a moment. ^Ready? B, because it was added first. First in, first out, and that ordering is the entire reason this finds a shortest path.

quiz.question: B and C are queued. Which is checked first?
quiz.why: First in, first out. That ordering is what makes it shortest.

scenes.headline: B, and the [second ring]
scenes.caption: distance two appears
scenes.narration: |We take ^B off the front, %one stop out, and it's not our destination. B connects to ^D, which hasn't been seen, |so we mark it and push it on the back at two stops. +The queue is now C at one, then D at two. C was added before D, so C gets looked at first, even though we're standing beside D. So the queue refuses to let's run ahead, which is exactly what keeps the distances in order.

lines.detail: D goes on the back, at two stops.

scenes.headline: Why [visited] matters
scenes.caption: C finds D already taken
scenes.narration: |Now C comes off the front, ^also one stop out, and it isn't our destination either. C connects to D as well, and here the code does something that looks like nothing. |D is %already in the visited set, so we skip it. Without that skip D gets queued twice, and on a map with a loop the search never finishes.

lines.detail: Already visited, so skip it. This is the guard.

scenes.headline: D, and the [last hop]
scenes.caption: E joins the queue
scenes.narration: |D comes off the front at ^two stops. Still not our destination. D connects to ^E, and E is new, |so we mark it and push it on at two plus one, which is three stops. +E is now the only thing waiting. Distances have climbed in order the whole way: zero, one, one, two, three. The queue kept them sorted without a single comparison.

lines.detail: Take D from the front, at two stops.
E goes on at three stops.

scenes.premise: A subway map. Each circle is a station, each line a direct connection, and the badge on a station is how many stops it sits from A.

scenes.headline: Arrived, in [three stops]
scenes.caption: the answer
scenes.narration: |E comes off the front, ^three stops out. Every station nearer than three has already been taken off and dealt with, |so when we ask whether E is our destination, and it is, we return the distance it carried: %three. We compared no routes at all, because the first arrival is the shortest arrival.

lines.detail: Arrived. Return the distance it carried.

scenes.headline: Queue, or [stack]
scenes.caption: one word, two algorithms
scenes.narration: Here's what to remember when you're tired and under pressure. ^Take from the front and you've breadth-first search, which fans out in rings and gives you shortest. ^Take from the back and you've depth-first search, which dives down one branch. ^Popleft is BFS. ^Pop is DFS. ^And BFS costs memory, because a wide ring is a big queue. Same code, one word different, completely different answer, and that trade is worth naming before anybody asks you for it.

scenes.narration: Three things to take with you. Your signal is %shortest, or minimum steps. Reach for a %queue and a visited set, always both. And the reason it works is that %the first arrival is the shortest arrival.

Next in the Dojo is depth-first search and backtracking: the same code with one word changed, and a completely different personality, because taking from the back turns rings into a dive. Go and do Level Order first.
